title: The Trap of Spiritual Highs — Luke 9:33
paragraphs: The Trap of Spiritual Highs — Luke 9:33
Peter was not backslidden in Luke 9:33.
He was overwhelmed.

On the mountain, Jesus was transfigured. Glory burst through the ordinary. Moses. Elijah. Radiance. Wonder. And Peter said, “Master, it is good for us to be here. Let us make three tents…” (Luke 9:33).
That sounds spiritual.
But it was a trap.

Peter wanted to build a shelter around a moment God never asked him to preserve. He wanted to stay where it felt powerful, bright, undeniable. No demons screaming. No crowds pressing. No cross in sight. Just glory.
And that is still our temptation.

We chase the conference high.
The worship tears.
The altar moment.
The goosebumps.
We call it depth.
Sometimes it is just escape.

Because spiritual highs can feel holy while quietly teaching us to love the feeling of God more than the will of God. Peter wanted a mountain. Jesus was headed to a cross. Peter wanted to freeze the revelation. Jesus came to fulfill redemption.
But here’s what we miss:
The Father interrupted Peter.

Not with applause.
With a command.
“This is My beloved Son. Hear Him!” (Luke 9:35)

Hear Him when the moment is blazing.
Hear Him when the feeling fades.
Hear Him when obedience costs more than ecstasy.

The Christian life is not built on living from one spiritual rush to another. It is built on following Jesus down the mountain, into the valley, into the battle, into the slow, costly beauty of surrender.
That is where many believers stumble.
They think God left because the fire-feeling lifted.

No, beloved.
He did not leave.
He was just calling you deeper than emotion.

A faith that only survives in moments of intensity is still fragile. But a faith rooted in Christ will stand in silence, confusion, waiting, weakness, and warfare. Jesus is not only Lord of the mountain peak. He is Lord in the plain places too.
And that’s where grace walks in.
Because when we idolize spiritual highs, Jesus does not cast us off. He corrects us. He leads us. He teaches us to stop worshiping the experience and start obeying the Son.
The goal was never the tent.
The goal was always Christ.

So if you feel dry today, do not panic. Do not mistake the absence of emotional intensity for the absence of God. Open your Bible. Hear the Son. Obey the Son. Follow the Son. The real miracle is not that you felt something last night. It is that Jesus is still faithful this morning.

That is mature devotion.
That is discipleship.
That is grace.
